The year plays by itself: ❚❚ pauses it, ▶ starts it again, and the *Speed* slider sets how many days pass in one second. The buttons *20 March*, *21 June*, *23 September* and *21 December* stop Earth at an equinox or a solstice. The orbit is coloured by the seasons of the northern hemisphere. The panel *Seen from the side* gives the latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon and the length of the day in Neuchâtel; under the controls, the date and the season in each hemisphere.

## What to look for

- Watch the axis (N) during a whole year: does it ever change direction?
- Stop at 21 June, then at 21 December: which hemisphere leans towards the Sun? Where is the Sun overhead at noon?
- On 20 March and 23 September, where is the Sun overhead, and how long is the day in Neuchâtel?
- When it is summer in the northern hemisphere, what season is it in the southern hemisphere? Why?
- Count the days between the four dates of the buttons: are the four seasons equally long?

## How it works

The axis is tilted by 23.44° and keeps the same direction all year, so the latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon moves between the two tropics. Earth moves a little faster in January, when it is nearest to the Sun, but the orbit is drawn as a circle; distances, sizes and the spin of Earth are not to scale. The length of the day in Neuchâtel (47° N) runs from sunrise to sunset, with the usual allowance for the refraction of the air and the size of the Sun.
